records.name: Japan
records.summary:
Japan is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — the 2023 "understanding" law is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the Supreme Court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and the capital and the second city have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs (onsen) — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

sources.summary: Official translation of Japan's SOGI-promotion Act (Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity): defines 'gender identity', requires the government to publish annual implementation status of policies promoting understanding of SOGI diversity, and sets out the national basic plan — the statutory framework now governing official态度 to LGBT issues.

AP (Jul 2023): 'Japan's top court says government restrictions on transgender employee's use of restrooms illegal' — the Supreme Court upholds damages over a ministry's limits on a trans female employee's toilet access.

AP: 'A Japanese court rules it's unconstitutional to require surgery for a change of gender on documents' — landmark ruling in 'Gen Suzuki's' case against the sterilising-surgery requirement for legal gender-marker changes.

HRW (18 Jul 2023): Japan's Supreme Court ruled the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry violated public-service law by barring a transgender woman from the women's bathroom at work — she challenged the denial in 2015; a Tokyo district court had ruled for her in 2019 on her 'important legal interest' to live by her self-identified gender and awarded damages.

Kyodo News FOCUS (21 Jun 2023): Japan enacted its LGBT-understanding-promotion law after months of debate but the text was watered down amid a culture-war debate over transgender issues — documents the political contestation behind the statute.

Japan Cheapo inclusive-onsen guide: bathhouses (onsen, sento, super-sento) can be daunting for non-binary and trans visitors; provides LGBTQ+-friendly venue recommendations, private-bath and co-ed-pool options, and practical etiquette — a direct visitor-utility page for gender-diverse travelers.

Freely AU first-person guide 'Using onsen in Japan as a trans person' (published 29 Mar 2023, last updated 10 Jul 2026): what to expect using bathhouses as a trans traveller — practical expectations, venue norms and transition-related concerns from lived experience.

Japan Gay Guide visitor outlook: most travelers experience little direct hostility or discrimination, especially in major tourist destinations; LGBTQ visibility is low, social attitudes can be reserved, and legal equality still lags other developed countries — the standard visitor-risk posture for Japan.

records.name: Thailand
records.summary:
Thailand is one of Asia's most accepting destinations for transgender visitors. Visible gender variance is part of mainstream culture (the kathoey tradition long predates modern categories), the state actively promotes LGBTQ tourism, same-sex marriage became legal in January 2025 as the first in Southeast Asia, and the Immigration Bureau runs a dedicated "Welcome Pride" initiative to smooth entry for travellers whose passports don't match their appearance or gender. Gender-affirming healthcare is a mature, accessible industry.

The gaps are legal rather than social: there is still no procedure to change one's legal gender marker, the 2015 Gender Equality Act is weakly enforced, and — as the 2025 murder of a Thai trans woman in Pattaya highlighted — Thailand has no hate-crime law, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted as ordinary crime.

For a visitor the practical risks are mostly Thailand's general ones: nightlife disputes, scams, and alcohol-fuelled incidents, with some reported friction in resort nightlife districts. Everyday movement, hotels, healthcare, and trans

sources.summary: Thai Government PRD (05/08/2024): the Immigration Bureau launched 'Welcome Pride by Immigration' to mitigate concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports don't match their current appearance or gender — the entry-friction fix a trans visitor most needs to know about before arrival.

Outright International country overview (last updated Mar 12, 2026): Thailand became the first country in Southeast Asia to legalise same-sex marriage — bill passed its final Senate reading June 2024, in effect January 22, 2025, using gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms; its at-a-glance tables also carry the legal-status read.

Bangkok Post 'Pride in Action' forum (Lido Connect, 2025): advocates urge the government to expedite a gender-recognition law following marriage-equality, with public education framed as part of expanding rights protection — legal gender recognition is still pending post-SSM.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Nov 2025): when a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya in April, the community called it a hate crime but Thai law has no hate-crime designation — bias-motivated violence is handled as ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties or data collection; documents the accountability gap.

Globe (05/05/2025): following the Pattaya killing of a Thai trans woman by 42-year-old Chinese citizen Fu Tongyung after she refused his request for sex, LGBTQ+ groups urgently called for new hate-crime protections — names the perpetrator/victim facts and the resulting legal-protection push.

HRW report 'People Can't Be Fit into Boxes' (Dec 2021): no route for transgender people to obtain legal documentation reflecting their gender identity; even affirmative measures like first-name change leave discretionary power with officials; anti-discrimination protections are not fully enforced — the documentation gap a trans visitor may also feel.

NZZ in English (May 2025): the conservative government introduced progressive trans laws including free hormone treatments with little public opposition; trans people report greater societal acceptance and higher company positions than typical in the West — explains why social climate outruns the legal framework.

LegalClarity (June 2026): marriage equality since January 2025 and anti-discrimination law since 2015, yet no mechanism to change the sex marker on birth certificate, national ID or passport (title prefixes locked to sex at birth; Name Act 1962 partial workaround) — precise current documentation-status read.

records.name: Mexico
records.summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comp

sources.summary: HRW dispatch (31 March 2025) "Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges": calls on Mexico’s states to guarantee administrative legal gender recognition — many states now have LGR procedures, but without recognition, document requests expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation; implementation gaps persist state to state.

HRW report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024), Tabasco: barriers to legal name/gender recognition leave trans people exposed — document mismatch amplifies daily discrimination, set against murders including a trans woman found in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

The Guardian (18 July 2024): Mexico City’s Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" criminalising transfemicide — a watershed named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists say the law is critical for feeling safe.

AP (Jan 2024): 'Wave of transgender killings in Mexico spurs protests' — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca shot in Mexico City, drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.

IACHR press release (2024): urges federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanding investigation of all LGBTI violations with gender-identity-respecting methods; warns impunity may reach alarming levels.

Agencia Presentes (Jun 2024): 'Violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders increased in the last year' in Mexico — data report on rising attacks against trans people and killings of defenders.

LSE USAPP analysis by Caroline Beer (22 November 2024): Mexico’s progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly — rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; the authors explicitly caution their earlier work must not be read as evidence LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence including murder and torture.

Global Affairs Canada travel advice for Mexico: "Exercise a high degree of caution" nationwide due to high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with regional "avoid non-essential travel" advisories (e.g. Baja California Sur and the northwestern mainland coast); recently updated for Hurricane Polo.

records.name: Portugal
records.summary:
Portugal remains one of the world's safest destinations for transgender visitors. The 2018 self-determination law allows legal gender and name change without medical requirements (minors 16-17 with parental consent), bathroom access matching one's gender is legally protected, conversion therapy is banned (2024), intersex infant surgery is banned, and hate-crime law covers gender identity — within an EU rule-of-law environment with very low violent crime. Same-sex marriage since 2010.

Two caveats pull it just below its Iberian neighbour Spain. First, in March 2026 the Portuguese parliament approved in first reading three bills (backed by the governing PSD/CDS and the far-right Chega) that would repeal the 2018 self-ID law, reintroduce a mandatory medical opinion, and ban hormones for minors. As of the most recent reporting this is not yet final law — it is in committee, and a government technical opinion warned it may be unconstitutional — so the self-ID framework is still in force. Second, hate-crime reports rose about 38% in both 2023 and 2024, with acknowledged under-repor

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map 2026: Portugal drops one place to 12th at 67%; no affirmative legislation since the 2024 conversion-practices ban, while a new draft bill threatens legal gender recognition based on self-determination and the ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children. No score 67% below Malta/Iceland/Belgium but above most of Europe.
Público (March 2026, in Portuguese): the Portuguese Parliament (AR) approved PSD, Chega and CDS bills reversing the gender-identity law - first vote to roll back self-ID legal gender recognition.

Observador (Mar 2026): parliament debates rolling back the gender-identity regime; psychologists' order and trans groups call it 'retrocesso'; socialists invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta (trans woman killed by youths in Porto) against the rollback, drawing protests from Chega's Hugo Soares. Documents the political fight around the three roll-back bills.

Joint statement: IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal warn three bills debated 19 March, voted 20 March 2026 would seriously attack trans/intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition; if adopted Portugal would lose at least 4 Rainbow Map places, dropping below Sweden, Netherlands, Ireland and France - regression from a European reference point.

Forbidden Colours (20 Mar 2026): Parliament passed the roll-back proposals 124 to 79 (backed by Chega, governing PSD and CDS-PP), sending them to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees; the proposals directly target Portugal's 2018 self-identification law. Called a dangerous turning point for fundamental rights.

KET Brussels (26 Mar 2026): in first reading Parliament backed reintroducing a mandatory medical opinion for any legal gender and name change, undoing the 2018 reform that allowed self-declaration from age 16; human rights groups say it is dismantling the self-determination law.

TVI/IOL: committee-stage analysis (CIG) of the bills warns they worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people and defends schools' existing discrimination-prevention duties; Bloco de Esquerda bill assessed as compatible with school human-rights obligations. Legislative-process detail on the roll-back package.

The Portugal Brief (16 Aug 2026): Justice Ministry data show legal sex/name changes climbing back toward the two-years-prior high-water mark, most in Lisbon (per Expresso) - even as Parliament advances bills to reimpose the medical requirement the 2018 self-determination law scrapped. Uptick before the expected tightening.

records.name: Ireland
records.summary:
Ireland is a calm, comfortable destination for transgender visitors. It was one of the first countries to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration — the 2015 Gender Recognition Act lets adults change their legal gender without medical requirements — and bathroom use is unrestricted. A hate-crime law covering sexual orientation and gender identity took effect at the end of 2024, equality law bans discrimination in employment, housing and services, and marriage equality was approved by referendum in 2015.

The caveats are stagnation and a mildly worsening climate rather than active rollback. The 2015 law is binary-only and long-promised reform (non-binary, under-16s) has stalled; transphobic hate speech remains uncriminalised after a 2024 government U-turn; a university study in 2025 documented rising discrimination against sexual and gender minorities; and total hate-crime reports rose about 15% in 2025 (racism and xenophobia are the most common motives). None of this amounts to criminal exposure or physical danger for a visitor.

sources.summary: Guardian (23 Dec 2025): decade retrospective on Ireland's gender recognition — the 2015 Act marked a move away from Ireland's Catholic past; first-person accounts of self-declaration and updated documents, alongside renewed calls over remaining gaps in trans rights and healthcare.

Irish Statute Book: Gender Recognition Act 2015 (No. 25 of 2015) — commenced 4 September 2015 (S.I. 369/2015); the operative statutory text enabling legal gender recognition, later amended per S.I. updates through 2026.

Belong To LGBTQ+ Youth Ireland: hate-crime guidance — anonymous online hate-crime reporting form, rights information and links to Equal Status Acts protections for young LGBTQ+ people reporting incidents.
thin: no usable finding

Irish Times (Aug 2026): Garda reports of hate crimes rose 15% in 2025 with racism and xenophobia the most common motives — under the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024, which explicitly covers gender identity and sex characteristics.

Irish Times (3 Jul 2025): UCD study finds discrimination against sexual and gender minorities in Ireland has increased — documented rise in anti-LGBTQ+ prejudice despite the protective statutory framework.

GCN (10 years on): self-declared gender recognition since the 2015 Act — Ireland is one of only 11 European countries allowing gender recognition through self-determination with no psychological evaluation requirement; activists mark the anniversary while flagging remaining gaps.
Outright International country overview: Ireland at-a-glance — same-sex relations legal nationwide for men and women, with the policy/legal-status matrix used as a baseline reference for the record.

records.name: Belgium
records.summary:
Belgium is a top-tier destination for transgender visitors. Legal gender and name change by self-declaration has been available since 2018, anti-discrimination law covers gender identity and expression across employment, housing and services, hate crime and hate speech are both criminalised for gender identity, and transphobia is a separately tracked hate-crime motive. Belgium also passed Europe's first femicide law (2023), with protections for gender minorities.

The framework is politically stable with no rollback movement — a contrast with several neighbours (the UK's in-force facilities code, Portugal's first-reading repeal attempt, Germany's repeal review). The main caveat is a documented rise in anti-LGBTQ violence and intimidation: the equality body Unia reported in 2025 that gay men and transgender people are increasingly targeted, and an RTBF investigation documented dating-app ambush attacks on queer men in urban nightlife.

For a visitor this is a comfortable environment with the usual urban-nightlife caution: zero legal exposure, functioning institut

sources.summary: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Belgium has robust protections - discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of SOGISC banned; same-sex marriage and adoption; legal name and gender-marker change based on self-determination. Europe's first femicide law (2023) covers all gender-based homicide; a 2023 law bans conversion practices. Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, though a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for nonconsensual interventions.

ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Belgium: overall index score plus per-category compliance (legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality & non-discrimination, family, civil society, asylum, intersex) — the formal-law snapshot of Belgium's framework.

VRT NWS (May 2025): despite Belgium's progressive reputation, equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men report rising violence and intimidation targeting LGBTQI people, with gay men and trans people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases handled by Unia in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. A recurring pattern is 'dating app traps' - gay men lured via apps, ambushed, beaten and robbed; a high-profile case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went to Brussels Criminal Court in May 2025.

KET Magazine (Feb 2025) summarising an RTBF investigation into rising homophobic attacks in Belgium orchestrated through dating apps: perpetrators use fake profiles to arrange meetings, then ambush victims in isolated locations where they are robbed, humiliated or assaulted. Police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported due to fear or shame.

OSCE/ODIHR page on Belgium's national hate-crime frameworks: hate crimes are not defined in Belgian legislation and no code exists to record them as such; violations of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions instead.

Official Brussels-Capital Region page on changing gender registration on ID cards: free of charge, 3-6 weeks processing, requires a valid identity document, a medical certificate attesting to sex change, and possibly a judicial or administrative decision; application made in person at the commune, digital mode available.

Belgian Federal Justice Department page: since 1 January 2018 (Law of 25 June 2017), trans people can change registered gender and first names without medical conditions, via a declaration to the civil registrar. On 19 June 2019 the Constitutional Court partially annulled the law; pending new provisions, applications continue under the current procedure.

Intrepid Travel country guide: Belgium is 'one of the safest and most welcoming destinations for LGBTQIA+ travellers in the world', with forward-thinking attitudes and thriving queer culture in Brussels, Antwerp and Liège.
